extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary criticism; those studying fiction, biography, and 17th–18th century French literary culture
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative principles for fiction and life-writing (esp. George Eliot and Carlyle) and criteria for assessing women’s literary production and salon-culture in 17th–18th century France.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unrelenting fidelity to human nature and human life
rubrics_metrics.description: “realness, her unrelenting fidelity to human nature and human life.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A high standard for fiction: portray characters with truthful, often painful realism rather than sentimentality. Example: George Eliot’s pathos in Tiny and Mrs. Amos Barton; anti-pattern: shallow caricature or mawkish sentiment that avoids the truth of human difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative sympathy / 'thinking herself imaginatively into the experience of others'
rubrics_metrics.description: “the habit of thinking herself imaginatively into the experience of others.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiction should create knowledge of others by feeling with them; requires an authorial imagination that inhabits diverse experiences. Effect: makes novels come home pitilessly to readers who have deep life experience; downside: can fascinate and alienate some readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose the peculiar combination of outward and inward facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to disclose “the peculiar combination of outward with inward facts which constitute a man’s critical actions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate character by showing how external circumstances and inner motives combine to produce actions. Guidance: avoid premature moral judgment until the combination is known; this disclosure is central to deep character-delineation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delicate, subtle, and far-in analysis of motive
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis should be “delicate, subtle, and far-in.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depth of psychological analysis is a virtue; it creates an atmosphere (here, sadness) distinct from authors who show only external behavior. Contrast with more surface-level comic or purely behavioral portrayals (e.g., Dickens’ emphasis on behavior).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of humour and pathos (pensive undertone)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The humor of Mrs. Poyser and the wit of Mrs. Transome only deepen the pathos by relieving it. There is hardly a sarcasm in these books but has its pensive undertone.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comic elements not to undermine seriousness but to deepen emotional effect; sarcasm should carry an underlying sympathy or pensiveness rather than mere mockery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charity and avoidance of 'served him right' moralizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Absence of the spirit of “served him right,” “just what she deserved,” or “they ought to have known better.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judgmental or punitive moralizing is an anti-pattern; a charitable, understanding stance toward characters is preferred, recognizing coercions and complexities that lead to moral error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisites for ideal life-writing
rubrics_metrics.description: “The conditions required for the perfection of life writing—personal intimacy, a loving and poetic nature which sees the beauty and the depth of familiar things, and the artistic power which seizes characteristic points and renders them with lifelike effect—are seldom found in combination.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good biography needs (1) intimacy with the subject, (2) a sympathetic/poetic sensibility, and (3) artistic skill to pick and render telling details. This rare conjunction explains why exemplary lives are uncommon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selectivity: tell neither too little nor too much
rubrics_metrics.description: “We are told neither too little nor too much; the facts noted, the letters selected, are all such as serve to give the liveliest conception of what Sterling was and what he did.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biographical material should be curated to serve the main purpose—include facts and documents that give the liveliest conception; avoid overloading readers with irrelevant detail or leaving out essential formative facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collateral matter as scene-painting accessory
rubrics_metrics.description: Collateral matter (portraits of other persons, incidents) should be “all a kind of scene-painting, and is accessory to the main purpose.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use portraits and contextual material to illuminate the subject, not distract; every tangent should help reveal the biographee’s character or milieu.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic excellence in biography
rubrics_metrics.description: Style of the work should be “at once pure and rich; there are passages of deep pathos ... aptness of epithet, masterly power of close delineation.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate life-writing for clarity, richness, apt phrasing, and power of close portraiture; these produce pathos and vividness. Anti-pattern: dry compilation lacking stylistic vitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification for producing another life (supplement/correction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A second Life is justified where an earlier biography is incomplete or apologetic and a new account corrects or fills out the subject’s mental course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A new biography should add corrective perspective or substantial new material (not merely repeat); it should address gaps or misrepresentations of previous accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge sex-differences in literature (distinctive feminine contribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: “We think it an immense mistake to maintain that there is no sex in literature... woman has something specific to contribute.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism and creation should recognize that women may bring distinctive perspectives (e.g., maternal sensations, different affective textures). Evaluate works with attention to those specific contributions rather than forcing a male-model standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity: write in habitual language, not imitating men
rubrics_metrics.description: French women “wrote...in their habitual language, without proposing any model to themselves, without any intention to prove that women could write as well as men, without affecting manly views or suppressing womanly ones.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value naturalness and voice rooted in lived experience; anti-pattern: literary production that imitated masculine mannerisms or adopted an affected, competitive posture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity, lightness, and avoidance of prolixity
rubrics_metrics.description: Women’s salons fostered “the combination of the utmost exaltation in sentiment with the utmost simplicity of language... an instinctive fondness for lightness of treatment and airiness of expression, thus making them cut short all prolixity and reject all heaviness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concise, airy expression and simplicity of diction in certain genres; verbose or heavy treatment often weakens the charm and accessibility of writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation (the degeneration into précieuses ridicules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affectation replaces simplicity; the _genre précieux_ degenerated into affectation, giving rise to satire such as _Les Femmes Savantes_ and _Précieuses Ridicules_.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware stylistic and social affectation—artificial ornament or forced refinement is an anti-pattern that invites ridicule and undermines genuine taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candour in portraiture
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Palais du Luxembourg portraits, defects and virtues were to be spoken of “with like candor.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portrait-poetry and personal sketches succeed when candidly balancing virtues and faults; candor increases interest (and social curiosity) and may help create a new manner of writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salon inclusivity and conversational breadth as cultural fuel
rubrics_metrics.description: Salons were réunions of both sexes with conversation on the whole gamut of subjects and included hommes d’affaires and soldiers as well as authors; this diversity refined taste and produced a new standard of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural and literary vitality benefits from inclusive, wide-ranging conversation across social types and topics; anti-pattern: insular or purely literary coteries that stifle practical intelligence and variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual / historical evaluation of literary achievement
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare authors within their historical material: seventeenth-century women had more exaltation and less self-consciousness; eighteenth-century writers had a richer fund of ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess writers relative to their epoch’s resources and social conditions rather than by anachronistic standards; what counts as achievement may differ by period.
